os-traffic.title: From monthly users to peak requests per second
os-traffic.description: An example of 20,000 monthly active users becoming 6,000 people on a workday, 240,000 requests a day, and 25 requests per second at peak.
os-traffic.note: Replace each assumption with numbers from your logs once you have them.

os-database.title: Limits to check before adding a second database
os-database.description: Four specific limits that often give out before a relational database runs out of total capacity: a missing index, the connection limit, a long transaction, and memory.
os-database.note: Common suspects, not a ranking: your own benchmark shows which one you hit.

os-monolith.title: Pressures that justify extracting a service
os-monolith.description: Four separate pressures that can justify moving a module out of a monolith: team coordination, deploy conflicts, independent scaling, and failure isolation.
os-monolith.note: If you cannot name one of these, keep it a module with a clear interface.

os-cache-queue.title: Fixes to try before adding a cache
os-cache-queue.description: The order to try fixes for a slow read: fix the query, add an index, precompute a summary table, and only then add a cache.
os-cache-queue.note: For slow background work, the same logic puts a job table ahead of a broker.

os-availability.title: Monthly downtime budget for each availability target
os-availability.description: The minutes of downtime allowed in a 30-day month at 99%, 99.5%, 99.9%, and 99.99% availability.
os-availability.note: Based on a 30-day month. A 500 GB restore at 100 MB/s takes about 83 minutes.

os-reversible.title: What is hard to undo, and what can wait
os-reversible.description: Three decisions that are hard to undo, the data model, public APIs, and data ownership, beside a cache or broker, which is easier to add later.
os-reversible.note: Spend early effort on the hard ones. Write a revisit trigger for the rest.
